---
title: "How results are validated"
description: >
  The oracles, fixtures, manifest, and tolerances behind every knappnet
  measure, and how documented differences with other tools are recorded.
---

A network measure is only useful if its numbers can be trusted, and in
published work they will be checked. knappnet does not ask to be taken on
trust. Every measure is compared, on every change to the code, with
independent computations of the same quantity, and every disagreement
either fails the build or is recorded with its reason. Everything
described here lives in the
[`validation/`](https://github.com/knapply/knappnet/tree/main/validation)
directory of the repository and can be rerun by anyone.

## Oracles

An *oracle* is an independent source of the right answer. Each measure is
checked against every oracle that implements it:

- **Reference tools.** [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) and [sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna) in R, and [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) in Python, run as
  black boxes on the same networks
  ([`validation/oracles/`](https://github.com/knapply/knappnet/tree/main/validation/oracles)).
- **Definitions.** Slow, deliberately simple implementations written
  directly from the textbook formula, sharing no code with the engine, and
  using exact rational arithmetic where possible (for example, betweenness
  by counting shortest paths with exact fractions, and eigenvector
  centrality by a dense eigendecomposition). These are the strongest evidence of correctness: a
  definition oracle does not inherit any tool's conventions or bugs.
- **Exact enumeration.** QAP p-values are checked on small networks by
  evaluating all n! relabelings, so they are compared exactly rather than
  within simulation error
  ([`validation/qap_check.py`](https://github.com/knapply/knappnet/blob/main/validation/qap_check.py)).

[UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) runs only as a Windows program and cannot run unattended. Its
conventions are implemented from its documentation and from the port of
its routines by its authors; comparisons against golden files produced by
UCINET itself are reported separately and will be added.

## Fixtures

The same corpus of networks
([`validation/fixtures/`](https://github.com/knapply/knappnet/tree/main/validation/fixtures))
goes to every oracle. It is generated deterministically by
`validation/fixtures.py`, and CI checks that regenerating it changes
nothing. It includes:

- **Classic data:** Zachary's karate club, Padgett's Florentine families,
  Davis's Southern women, Krackhardt's kite, and Knuth's Les Misérables
  co-appearances (weighted).
- **Random networks** across densities, directed and undirected.
- **Weights of every kind the engine treats differently:** all equal
  (which must reduce exactly to the unweighted case), small whole numbers
  (bucket queue with exact integer distances), and arbitrary real numbers
  (Dijkstra's algorithm).
- **Edge cases:** an empty network, a single node, a pair, stars, paths,
  complete graphs, directed cycles, isolates, and networks with self-loops
  and parallel edges, where tools most often disagree.

## The manifest

[`validation/manifest.yaml`](https://github.com/knapply/knappnet/blob/main/validation/manifest.yaml)
(with one file per area in `validation/manifest.d/`) lists every measure:
the engine call being validated, the networks it applies to, the numerical
tolerance, and each oracle's equivalent call. An entry looks like this:

```yaml
degree_all:
  engine: {fn: degree, mode: all, loops: true}
  applies_to: any
  tolerance: {rel: 0, abs: 0}
  oracles:
    definition:
      call: "direct evaluation of the definition (validation/oracles/definition_oracle.py)"
    networkx:
      call: "MultiGraph/MultiDiGraph G.degree()"
    igraph:
      call: "igraph::degree(g, mode = 'all', loops = TRUE)"
    sna:
      call: "sna::degree(m, gmode, cmode = 'freeman' | 'indegree' for graphs)"
      differs_when: [loops, multi_edges]
      reason: >-
        sna works on adjacency matrices, so parallel edges collapse to one,
        and it ignores the diagonal by default (diag = FALSE).
```

No measure ships without a manifest entry and at least one passing oracle.

### Tolerances

Counts and integer results (degree, the triad census, components, cliques,
cores) must match exactly: the tolerance is zero. Floating-point results
are compared with a relative and an absolute tolerance chosen for the
computation, typically 10<sup>-9</sup> to 10<sup>-12</sup> for path-based
measures and 10<sup>-8</sup> for iterative ones such as eigenvector
centrality, whose reference tools stop at their own convergence
thresholds. Partitions (community labels) are compared up to relabeling,
and collections such as cliques as sets.

### Outcomes

[`validation/compare.py`](https://github.com/knapply/knappnet/blob/main/validation/compare.py)
compares the engine with every oracle on every fixture and classifies
each comparison:

| Outcome | Meaning |
|---|---|
| match | Values agree within the tolerance. |
| documented | Values differ on a network where the manifest declares a convention difference for that oracle, with the reason. |
| FAIL | Any other disagreement. The build fails. |
| undefined | The oracle gives no answer on that network (it raises an error, or the quantity is undefined there), as declared in the manifest. |
| not run | No result from that oracle. In CI, every automated oracle must run. |

The results are written to
[`validation/REPORT.md`](https://github.com/knapply/knappnet/blob/main/validation/REPORT.md),
which lists each measure against each oracle and spells out every
documented difference.

## Documented differences

A documented difference is never a silent pass: it applies only on
networks with the declared property, only for the named oracle, and only
with a stated reason. Some examples from the manifest:

- **[sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna), degree, on networks with loops or parallel edges.** sna works on
  adjacency matrices, so parallel edges collapse to one and the diagonal is
  ignored. `degree(g, convention = "sna")` reproduces sna and is validated
  against it.
- **[NetworkX](https://networkx.org/), betweenness, on multigraphs.** NetworkX traverses neighbor
  sets, so parallel edges count as a single shortest path; [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) and
  knappnet count each parallel edge as a distinct path.
  `convention = "networkx"` reproduces NetworkX.
- **igraph, normalized betweenness, with fewer than three nodes.** The
  normalizing constant is zero. igraph returns `NaN`; knappnet, like
  NetworkX, returns 0, since no node can lie between two others.
- **NetworkX, weighted betweenness with reciprocal weights.** Reciprocals
  of whole-number weights often give path lengths that tie exactly
  (1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2) but differ in the last bit of floating point. NetworkX
  compares lengths exactly and drops one of the tied paths. knappnet, like
  igraph, compares with a relative tolerance, and agrees with the
  exact-arithmetic definition oracle.
- **NetworkX, modularity of a network without edges.** Modularity is
  undefined there; NetworkX returns 0, knappnet and igraph `NaN`.

Several documented differences, like the last two, come from the
reference tool rather than from knappnet: the definition oracle sides with
knappnet. The [conventions guide](conventions.html) explains the
differences an analyst is most likely to meet.

## Beyond the manifest

- **Property tests** in the engine check invariants on hundreds of random
  networks each: relabeling nodes permutes the results, unit weights reproduce
  unweighted results, strengths w give the same results as distances 1/w,
  every shortest-path algorithm gives the same answer on the same lengths,
  and the number of threads changes no result beyond floating-point
  rounding.
- **File formats** are checked in both directions against [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/)'s and
  [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/)'s own readers and writers
  ([`validation/io_check.py`](https://github.com/knapply/knappnet/blob/main/validation/io_check.py)).
  DyNetML, which neither reads, is tested against its specification.
- **Benchmarks are correctness checks too.** Every timing in the
  [performance guide](performance.html) compares the two tools' answers,
  and the run fails if they differ.
- **The README's examples** are rerun in R on every change, and the build
  fails if any printed output drifts.
- **R CMD check** runs the package's tests, which repeat key comparisons
  against igraph and [sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna) from R, on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

## Running it yourself

From the repository root, with Rust, Python (with networkx, numpy, scipy,
and PyYAML), and R (with [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/), [sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna), and yaml):

```sh
python3 validation/fixtures.py           # regenerate fixtures (deterministic)
python3 validation/run_oracles.py        # golden values from every oracle
python3 validation/compare.py            # compare; writes validation/REPORT.md
python3 validation/io_check.py           # file formats
python3 validation/qap_check.py          # QAP against exact enumeration
```

Golden files are committed together with the versions of the oracles that
produced them, and regenerated when an oracle's version changes. All of
this runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows for every change.
